title: A signal after a meal
q: Which hormone from pancreatic beta cells can increase glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue?
why: Insulin released by pancreatic beta cells can increase glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue and helps reduce blood glucose.

title: A signal between meals
q: Which hormone from pancreatic alpha cells promotes glucose release by the liver?
why: Glucagon released by pancreatic alpha cells promotes liver glucose output, including through glycogen breakdown and glucose production.

title: A signal about water
q: Which hormone released from the posterior pituitary can increase water reabsorption in kidney collecting ducts?
why: ADH can increase collecting-duct water permeability and reabsorption. It is produced in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

title: A signal about sodium
q: Which adrenal-cortex hormone promotes sodium reabsorption in the kidney?
why: Aldosterone acts on parts of the kidney to promote sodium reabsorption and influences potassium secretion.

title: A signal about calcium
q: Which hormone from the parathyroid glands helps raise blood calcium through actions involving bone and kidney?
why: Parathyroid hormone helps raise blood calcium through effects involving bone, kidney and activation of vitamin D. The diagram shows selected targets only.

title: Another calcium signal
q: Which hormone released by thyroid C cells can lower blood calcium by inhibiting bone resorption?
why: Calcitonin can inhibit bone resorption and lower blood calcium; its physiological role in adult humans is less prominent than that of parathyroid hormone.

title: A gland signals another
q: Which anterior-pituitary hormone stimulates thyroid hormone production and release?
why: Thyroid-stimulating hormone, or TSH, stimulates the thyroid gland. Thyroid hormones participate in feedback regulation of the axis.

title: The first step of an axis
q: Which hypothalamic releasing hormone stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH?
why: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus stimulates TSH release from the anterior pituitary.

title: A signal to ovarian follicles
q: Which anterior-pituitary hormone helps stimulate ovarian follicle development?
why: Follicle-stimulating hormone helps stimulate ovarian follicle development. Ovarian function also depends on other hormones and feedback.

title: A surge before ovulation
q: A mid-cycle surge of which pituitary hormone helps trigger ovulation?
why: A surge in luteinizing hormone helps trigger ovulation in an ovulatory menstrual cycle. The diagram omits the rest of the feedback sequence.

title: A signal for milk production
q: Which anterior-pituitary hormone promotes milk production in mammary tissue?
why: Prolactin promotes milk production. Oxytocin has a different role in milk ejection.

title: A signal for milk release
q: Which hormone released from the posterior pituitary promotes milk ejection?
why: Oxytocin promotes milk ejection by acting on myoepithelial cells. It is produced in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

title: A signal to make red cells
q: Which hormone produced mainly by the kidneys stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow?
why: Erythropoietin produced largely by the kidneys stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow, including in response to low oxygen availability.

title: A signal for biological timing
q: Which pineal hormone helps signal timing of the light–dark cycle to the body?
why: The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which participates in circadian timing and reflects the light–dark cycle.

title: A longer stress signal
q: Which glucocorticoid hormone is released by the adrenal cortex and helps regulate metabolism during stress?
why: Cortisol is a glucocorticoid released by the adrenal cortex and participates in metabolic and stress responses. Its effects depend on context.

title: A rapid stress signal
q: Which adrenal-medulla hormone can increase heart rate during a sympathetic response?
why: The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine, which can increase heart rate as part of a sympathetic response.
